summary: Describes mappings of SNMP onto both the connection-oriented and connectionless OSI transport services. It is an Experimental document and was replaced by RFC 1418.

plainLanguage.summary: It lets the network-monitoring messages travel over a different family of network standards.

questions: how to run snmp over osi
how do you run snmp over osi
how does snmp work with osi transport services
subtitle: Running SNMP management traffic over OSI transport services instead of UDP.

tldr.problem: SNMP was designed primarily for TCP/IP networks, but many organizations were deploying OSI protocols and wanted to use their existing SNMP management infrastructure with OSI systems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1283 defines how to map SNMP onto both OSI connectionless transport (CLTS) and connection-oriented transport (COTS) services, using appropriate addressing conventions and transport selectors for each.
tldr.outcome: Network managers in OSI environments could leverage SNMP for management, though the protocol proved less widely adopted than TCP/IP. RFC 1418 replaced this with an updated mapping.

today: RFC 1283 is Experimental and is obsoleted by RFC 1418, which provides an updated mapping of SNMP to OSI transport services based on implementation experience.

sections.title: Background and Design Goals
sections.content:
RFC 1283, published in December 1991, defines how to run the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) over OSI transport services. While SNMP is primarily associated with TCP/IP networks, it was designed to be transport-independent. As organizations adopted OSI protocols to manage OSI equipment, this RFC provided the mapping rules to use SNMP as their management framework.

SNMP works over connectionless transport (like UDP in TCP/IP), and the RFC addresses both OSI connectionless transport service (CLTS) and connection-oriented transport service (COTS). The design avoids mapping SNMP to the OSI application layer; instead, it maps directly to OSI transport services to preserve the proven simplicity of the Internet management model.
sections.plainLanguage: When companies started using OSI networks, they wanted to use the same management tool (SNMP) they already had. This RFC shows how to make SNMP work with the OSI network services.

sections.title: OSI Transport Services and Addressing
sections.content:
OSI defines two fundamentally different transport services. Connectionless Mode Transport Service (CLTS) sends individual packets with full addressing, similar to UDP. Connection-Oriented Transport Service (COTS) requires establishing a connection before sending data, like TCP. Both can carry SNMP messages, but they require different handling and addressing conventions.

Unlike TCP/IP, which uses well-known port numbers, OSI uses opaque transport selectors for demultiplexing. For SNMP over CLTS based on CLNP, the transport selector is the four ASCII characters 'snmp', while SNMP traps go to the selector 'snmp-trap'. For COTS based on TP4/CLNP, the same selectors apply. For TP0/X.25-based COTS, X.25 protocol IDs are used instead.
sections.plainLanguage: OSI has two ways to send data: connectionless (fire and forget, like postcards) and connection-oriented (like a phone call). SNMP needs different settings for each one, and instead of port numbers, OSI uses 'selectors' (names for the destination).

sections.title: Mapping to CLTS and COTS
sections.content:
Mapping SNMP to CLTS is straightforward: the elements of procedure are identical to UDP transport, with one difference in the Trap PDU format. Each SNMP message is sent as a single packet with full addressing information (transport selector and network address).

COTS mapping is more complex because SNMP is not inherently connection-oriented. The mapping establishes a transport connection, sends one or more SNMP messages on that connection, and then releases it. The initiator should not require responses to be returned on the same connection. Connection release is typically initiated by the sender, though either side may close due to resource limits or timeout. The RFC emphasizes that reliability and retransmission of SNMP messages remain the responsibility of the SNMP application, not the transport layer.
sections.plainLanguage: For the postcard style (CLTS), it's easy: just send the SNMP message with the selector name. For the phone-call style (COTS), you call up, send one or more messages, and hang up when done.

sections.title: User Interface Conventions
sections.content:
RFC 1283 recommends using a textual string encoding for OSI presentation addresses (defined in a referenced standard) to maintain consistency across multiple transport backings. This syntax follows the pattern [<t-selector>/]<n-provider><n-address>[+<n-info>].

For example, a CLNP-based address might appear as snmp/NS+4900590800200038bafe00, where 'snmp' is the transport selector and the hexadecimal string is the network address (NSAP). For UDP-based addresses, the syntax would be Internet=cheetah.nyser.net+161+2, showing the hostname, port, and protocol. While the RFC recommends this scheme, it acknowledges that simpler addressing schemes (such as a plain hostname) may be preferable in practice.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of using random port numbers, the RFC recommends a standard way to write out network addresses so they work the same way across different systems.
